presented_options.A: 0 = OK, 1 = SQL error, 2 = storage/IO, 3 = CLI usage (CLI last because it's the rarest)
presented_options.B: 0 = OK, 1 = any error (SQL, CLI, or IO collapsed together), with stderr distinguishing the category
presented_options.D: 0 = OK, 1 = SQL error, 2 = CLI usage error, 3 = storage/IO error

answers.rationale: A minimal database CLI typically maps exit codes as 0=OK, 1=SQL error, 2=CLI usage error, 3=storage/IO error. This ordering is natural because CLI usage errors (e.g., invalid flag) are checked early, storage errors are rarer, and the numbering follows the order of evaluation. Option A swaps CLI last which contradicts common ordering patterns. Option B collapses all errors into code 1 which defeats the purpose of distinguishing categories. Option C uses sysexits.h values which is more Unix-daemon convention than typical for a small educational DB.

presented_options.A: statements run without any transaction; durability is deferred to a periodic checkpoint
presented_options.B: statements run under a long-running implicit transaction that commits only when the process exits
presented_options.C: statements inherit the transaction of the previous BEGIN if any was ever opened in the session
presented_options.D: each statement is implicitly wrapped in its own transaction that commits on success, matching BEGIN/COMMIT semantics

answers.rationale: Standard SQL behavior is auto-commit: each statement outside an explicit BEGIN/COMMIT block is implicitly wrapped in its own transaction. This is the universal default in relational databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL). Option A (no transaction at all) would lose durability. Option B (long-running implicit transaction) would be unusual and break isolation. Option C (inheriting previous BEGIN) contradicts how transaction boundaries work.

presented_options.A: ARIES-style WAL with explicit undo and redo records plus a separate dirty-page table checkpoint
presented_options.B: shadow paging: mutations go to a copy page; a pointer swap at commit promotes the copy atomically
presented_options.C: synchronous double-write: every page is written to a scratch region before being written to its home location
presented_options.D: an append-only write-ahead log, replayed at startup to re-apply committed transactions and drop the uncommitted suffix

answers.rationale: An append-only write-ahead log is the simplest durability mechanism for a small database. Committed transactions are logged, and at startup the log is replayed: committed records are re-applied and any uncommitted suffix (no COMMIT record) is discarded. Option A (ARIES-style WAL) is too complex for an educational minidb. Option B (shadow paging) is a valid but different approach. Option C (synchronous double-write) is a page-level technique, not a full recovery strategy.

presented_options.A: each record carries a CRC32; replay stops at the first record whose CRC fails to verify
presented_options.B: records are padded to a fixed 512-byte sector boundary; partial sectors are discarded
presented_options.C: records are written in pairs (main + mirror); replay prefers whichever pair verifies
presented_options.D: no per-record check; a single CRC covers the whole WAL file on clean shutdown

answers.rationale: A CRC32 checksum per WAL record is the standard lightweight integrity mechanism. Replay reads records sequentially and stops at the first CRC failure, which cleanly detects partial/torn writes. Option B (sector padding) is more of a filesystem-level technique. Option C (mirror pairs) adds complexity without clear benefit for a minimal system. Option D (single file CRC) would not protect individual records.

presented_options.A: a Volcano-style iterator tree: each operator exposes open/next/close and returns one row (or tiny batch) at a time
presented_options.B: push-based execution where operators drive their children forward via a single dataflow scheduler
presented_options.C: materialising execution: each operator fully computes its output set before the next operator starts reading
presented_options.D: vectorised/columnar execution where each operator produces and consumes batches of column vectors

answers.rationale: A Volcano-style (iterator/pull-based) execution model is the classic approach for educational and small database systems. Each operator implements open/next/close and returns one row at a time. This is simple to implement and reason about. Option B (push-based dataflow) is more complex. Option C (materializing) is a variant but less standard as a named model. Option D (vectorised/columnar) is a modern optimization technique used in analytical systems.

presented_options.A: an inverted list built lazily on first query and cached in memory
presented_options.B: a B-tree keyed by the composite (index_key, row_id); duplicates are naturally ordered by row_id
presented_options.C: a hash map keyed by the indexed value alone; collisions chain a Vec<RowId>
presented_options.D: a bitmap per distinct value; looked up with bitwise AND for compound predicates

answers.rationale: A B-tree keyed by (index_key, row_id) is the classic secondary index structure. This allows efficient point lookups and range scans while naturally handling duplicate index keys by ordering them by row_id. Option A (inverted list) is for full-text search. Option C (hash map) only supports equality lookups. Option D (bitmap) is for low-cardinality analytical queries.

presented_options.A: Filter and Project exist as separate types rather than being fused into one 'SelectExpr' operator
presented_options.B: IndexScan and SeqScan as two variants of a single ScanKind enum so the executor only has one Scan operator
presented_options.C: Update and Delete are distinct operators rather than one 'Mutate' operator parameterised by a kind
presented_options.D: SeqScan, IndexScan, Filter, Project, NestedLoopJoin, Sort, Limit, Insert, Update, Delete each as a distinct type

answers.rationale: In a minimal educational database, Filter and Project are typically fused into a single SelectExpr or similar combined operator rather than being separate physical operator types. Having them as distinct types would be over-engineering for a small system. Options B, C, and D all describe plausible design choices: ScanKind enum is elegant, distinct Update/Delete is common, and separate operator types is the classic textbook approach.

presented_options.A: inside the storage layer, which transparently redirects SeqScan calls through the index when available
presented_options.B: inside the parser, encoded as a special AST node when the WHERE clause mentions an indexed column
presented_options.C: inside the planner when lowering the logical plan to a physical plan; the parser only produces ASTs
presented_options.D: inside the executor at open() time, after consulting the catalog to see whether an index is applicable

answers.rationale: Index selection logically belongs in the planner during logical-to-physical plan conversion. The parser produces a logical AST; the planner examines the catalog to determine available indexes and chooses between SeqScan and IndexScan. Option A (transparent redirection in storage) blurs abstraction layers. Option B (in the parser) conflates parsing with optimization. Option D (at executor open time) is too late and mixes planning with execution.

presented_options.A: a single crate-wide error enum with one variant per source is the return type of top-level entry points; lower modules convert at their public boundary
presented_options.B: errors are propagated via panics with typed payloads and caught at the CLI via std::panic::catch_unwind
presented_options.C: errors are encoded as strings (Result<T, String>) so every caller formats them uniformly
presented_options.D: each subsystem defines its own error type; the CLI sees a Box<dyn Error> and pattern-matches on downcast

answers.rationale: A single crate-wide error enum with variants per source (IO, parse, type-check, runtime) is the idiomatic Rust approach. Lower modules convert their errors at their public boundary into this unified type. Option B (panics) is poor error handling. Option C (String errors) loses type information. Option D (Box<dyn Error> with downcasts) is fragile and loses the structured error information that Rust's type system provides.

presented_options.A: table / csv / json selectable via a --format CLI flag or a .format meta-command in the REPL
presented_options.B: table output only; downstream callers are expected to parse and re-format it themselves
presented_options.C: the format is fixed at build time via a Cargo feature (--features=json)
presented_options.D: table / json / messagepack selectable only via an environment variable MINIDB_FORMAT

answers.rationale: A minimal database CLI typically supports table (human-readable), csv (machine-readable), and json (structured) output formats. These are selectable via a --format CLI flag and/or a .format meta-command in the REPL for interactive use. Option B (table only) is too limiting. Option C (compile-time feature) is inflexible. Option D (environment variable only) is unconventional for CLI tools.

presented_options.A: the per-statement summary is written to stdout immediately before the data so callers see it arrive first
presented_options.B: per-statement summary lines (e.g. `ok 3 rows`) go to stderr, letting callers pipe stdout straight into another tool
presented_options.C: --quiet suppresses the per-statement summary entirely; stdout still carries the data stream
presented_options.D: when --format json is active, the JSON value is the only thing on stdout — no banner lines, no trailing 'ok' line

answers.rationale: Writing per-statement summary to stdout BEFORE the data is inconsistent with the separation of data output (stdout) from progress output (stderr). The summary is progress/status information and should go to stderr (option B), be suppressible with --quiet (option C), or be absent when machine-readable format is active (option D). Mixing status lines into stdout would break piping.

presented_options.A: the heap stores rows inside fixed-size pages rather than one file per row
presented_options.B: pages are identified by a newtype over u64 (PageId) rather than a bare integer
presented_options.C: the page size is a single compile-time constant referenced throughout storage
presented_options.D: pages are a mixed size; the header chooses between 4 KiB and 16 KiB per table based on row width

answers.rationale: Mixed page sizes (4 KiB vs 16 KiB chosen per table) is inconsistent with how a minimal database typically organizes storage. A single compile-time constant page size (option C) is standard for simplicity. Options A (fixed-size pages) and B (PageId newtype) are both standard Rust practices for storage layers. Variable page sizes add significant complexity for page management and would be unusual in a minimal implementation.

presented_options.A: an error at startup demanding manual recovery before any SELECT can run
presented_options.B: all three rows — every fsynced WAL record is replayed on startup
presented_options.C: no rows — a transaction whose WAL trail has no COMMIT record is treated as an uncommitted prefix and discarded
presented_options.D: the two earliest rows — only WAL records that survive the CRC check are replayed; the trailing one is dropped

answers.rationale: If the COMMIT record was never written, the transaction is considered uncommitted. On recovery, WAL records without a trailing COMMIT are treated as an uncommitted prefix and discarded. This is standard WAL-based recovery semantics. Option A (error requiring manual recovery) is unnecessarily disruptive. Option B (all rows visible) would violate atomicity. Option D (partial replay based on CRC) conflates corruption detection with transaction recovery.

presented_options.A: a small number of hits inside `exec` operators, used to print per-row debugging during EXPLAIN
presented_options.B: hits only in `parser` and `error`, where the modules format diagnostic messages directly
presented_options.C: scattered hits across most modules; the codebase routinely uses `eprintln!` for diagnostics
presented_options.D: zero hits — every diagnostic outside the CLI boundary goes through the `log` facade

answers.rationale: In a well-structured Rust codebase, direct eprintln! usage outside the CLI boundary would be avoided in favor of the log facade (log crate with env_logger or similar). This keeps diagnostics configurable and filterable. Having scattered eprintln! calls (option C) would be considered poor practice. Having them only in parser/error (option B) or exec operators (option A) would still be inconsistent with using the log facade.

presented_options.A: panics with an unwrap on the unrecognised format string
presented_options.B: exits with code 2 and prints a CLI usage error on stderr naming the bad value
presented_options.C: exits with code 1 and prints a SQL error pointing at the SELECT
presented_options.D: executes the SELECT and silently falls back to the default `table` format

answers.rationale: An unrecognised --format value should be treated as a CLI usage error: exit with code 2 (matching Unix convention for usage errors) and print an error message on stderr naming the invalid value. Option A (panic) is not production-appropriate. Option C (SQL error code 1) misidentifies the source of the error. Option D (silent fallback) would be confusing since the user explicitly requested a format.
